title: The Best Pikachu Cards to Collect — Base Set to Pikachu ex, Raw to PSA 10, Dated Sold Prices | Gengar's Collector's Desk
description: Gengar's pick of the Pikachu cards that are true collectibles: Base Set Pikachu (1st Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited), Jungle and Neo Genesis Pikachu, the Skyridge holo, Pikachu ex from Ascended Heroes and Surging Sparks, the Crown Zenith gallery Pikachu, the 151 illustration rare, the Celebrations promos and an under-$10 shelf — each with dated raw, PSA 9, PSA 10 and TAG 10 sold prices and eBay links.
keywords: best pikachu cards, pikachu cards to collect, base set pikachu, pikachu ex ascended heroes, pikachu ex surging sparks, pikachu 151 illustration rare, most valuable pikachu cards, pikachu card collection
intro: Pikachu has more cards than any Pokémon, which makes this desk harder, not easier. Most of them are promos and filler. These are the ones a collector actually wants: the three Base Set prints, the Wizards-era holos nobody kept clean, and the handful of modern Pikachu ex cards that carry their sets.
narratorNote: I'll admit the mascot bores me a little. The cards don't. A Base Set Pikachu is a $3 card that becomes a three-figure slab in a 10 (four figures in 1st Edition), and that gap is the whole lesson of vintage collecting in one row. Every number here is a dated sold price from our own index data, every print is searched by its exact set and number, and nothing on this desk is a call to buy or sell.

shelves.label: The grails
shelves.blurb: Wizards-era Pikachus. Cheap raw, because everyone had one; expensive in a 10, because nobody kept one clean.

entries.title: Base Set Pikachu #58 (1999)
entries.why: The 1999 Pikachu, a common that every kid owned and almost nobody sleeved. Three prints — 1st Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited — with separate PSA labels and separate prices. The Unlimited raw is pocket money; the PSA 10 column is where this card becomes a collectible.

entries.title: Jungle Pikachu #60 (1999)
entries.why: The second English Pikachu, from Jungle. Same story as Base Set: a few dollars raw, a serious PSA 10. The 1st Edition is the print collectors chase.

entries.title: Neo Genesis Pikachu #70 (2000)
entries.why: The Neo Genesis Pikachu, from the set with the worst print quality of the Wizards run — which is exactly why its 10s are worth what they are.

entries.title: Skyridge Pikachu #84 (2003)
entries.why: Pikachu from the final Wizards set, one print run, one of the heaviest cards in our Skyridge index. The most expensive vintage Pikachu on this desk raw, by a distance.

shelves.label: The centerpieces
shelves.blurb: The modern Pikachus that carry their sets.

entries.title: Pikachu ex, Ascended Heroes (2026)
entries.why: The Special Illustration Rare #276 is the one of the heaviest cards in our Ascended Heroes index, up there with the Mega Gengar ex. The #277 is the same Pikachu ex in the other chase frame.

entries.title: Pikachu ex, Surging Sparks (2024)
entries.why: The Special Illustration Rare #238 is the heaviest card in our Surging Sparks index — a Pikachu set in name and in weight. The gold #247 and the #219 are the other chase frames; the regular #57 is on the starter shelf.

entries.title: Pikachu GG30 and #160, Crown Zenith (2023)
entries.why: Two Crown Zenith Pikachus: the GG30 from the Galarian Gallery illustration subset and the #160 from the main set's top end. Both under $50 raw with a PSA 10 many times that.

entries.title: Pikachu #173, Scarlet & Violet 151 (2023)
entries.why: The illustration-rare Pikachu from 151, one of the heavier cards in that index. One of the cards that made the 151 illustration rares a collecting lane of their own.

entries.title: Pikachu V SWSH145, Celebrations (2021)
entries.why: The Pikachu V promo from the 25th-anniversary Celebrations collection, one of the two heaviest cards in our Celebrations index. The SWSH143 is its sibling promo.

entries.title: Pikachu ex #150, 30th Celebration (2026)
entries.why: The 30th Celebration set has thirty Pikachu variants in it, and this is the ex at the top of them. The full lineup lives on our 30th Celebration page. Too new for graded marks that meet our rule.

entries.title: Van Gogh Pikachu (2023)
entries.why: The Pikachu with Grey Felt Hat promo from the Van Gogh Museum collaboration is the most-asked-about modern Pikachu and it has its own price page here: how much is the Van Gogh Pikachu worth. It is not in a set index, so it gets a link instead of a ladder on this desk.

shelves.label: The starter shelf
shelves.blurb: Pikachus for under $10 raw — and one that shows what a $6 card can do in a 10.

entries.title: Pikachu #5, Celebrations (2021)
entries.why: The Celebrations main-set Pikachu. Six dollars raw; look at the PSA 10 column, then at the TAG column.

entries.title: Flying and Surfing Pikachu VMAX, Celebrations (2021)
entries.why: The two Celebrations VMAX Pikachus, the Flying and the Surfing. A pair of fan-favourite forms for the price of a booster pack each.

entries.title: Pikachu ex #57, Surging Sparks (2024)
entries.why: The regular-art Pikachu ex from Surging Sparks, same card as the #238 SIR above in the plain frame.

entries.title: Pikachu #19, Hidden Fates (2019)
entries.why: The Hidden Fates main-set Pikachu. Two dollars raw, and a PSA 10 that is not two dollars.

collectingNotes.p: A Base Set Pikachu was a common. That is why the raw column on the vintage shelf is pocket money and the PSA 10 column is not: almost none were kept clean, so a gem copy of a card everyone owned is rarer than the holo it sat behind in the binder. The grading premium on vintage commons is among the biggest on this site.

1st Edition, Shadowless and Unlimited are three separate assets with separate PSA labels, separate population reports and separate price histories. Jungle and Neo Genesis split the same way into 1st Edition and Unlimited. Our indices track each print as its own card and every link here searches for the exact print on the row.

The Celebrations promos and the Van Gogh Pikachu are not set cards, and most Pikachu promos do not have the sales depth to mark. The ones on this desk are the ones that do; the Van Gogh page carries the one that trades outside any set.

PSA 10 is the hobby's price reference. TAG grades by machine-measured imaging with human review and publishes a full defect report for every card, which is why we link TAG slabs beside PSA on every row. We think measured grading is where the hobby is heading — our view, not a price claim. How TAG grading works →
